screens.title: Advanced Configuration Management with AWS Systems Manager
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will master the core pieces of AWS Systems Manager that let you manage large fleets and automate operational work. We'll look at the SSM Agent, how instances authenticate with an IAM instance profile, and four key capabilities: Run Command for remote execution, State Manager for enforcing desired state, Automation for orchestrating multi-step operations, and Parameter Store for secure configuration and secrets. You will see a hands-on pattern: create an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy, launch an EC2 instance with that role and verify the agent, author a small command document to install Nginx, and use State Manager to ensure the web server remains installed and running. This approach reduces manual SSH sessions, lowers your attack surface, and enforces consistency across environments. I will also warn you about common mistakes — forgetting the agent, missing IAM permissions, and untested associations — and show mitigation steps. By the end, you will understand each SSM capability, how they fit together in real operations, and how to apply them safely. What operational pain point will you solve first with SSM?

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Practical Outcomes
Verification checklist
  • SSM Agent installed and running on the instance.
  • Instance profile attached: AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore or equivalent.
  • Network egress allowed so the agent can reach SSM endpoints.
  • Test documents on an isolated group before global associations.
Audit: send Run Command output to S3 or CloudWatch for traceability.
Safety: use least-privilege IAM and parameter encryption with KMS.
Best practice
Always test association documents on a small set of instances and verify logs before scaling. This prevents conflicting associations and unintended restarts.

screens.title: SSM and the SSM Agent
screens.narratorSegment: The SSM Agent is a small daemon installed on EC2 instances and supported on some on-premises servers. Its role is simple but critical: it receives messages and documents from the Systems Manager control plane and executes actions on the host. Without the agent, SSM cannot discover or run commands on that instance. In practice you should think of the agent as the managed process that bridges your instance to the SSM service, relaying command inputs, execution progress, and output. For example, when you issue a Run Command to install a package, the SSM Agent runs the shell or PowerShell script and returns the result to the service, which can then forward logs to CloudWatch or S3. A common misconception is that SSM will manage any instance automatically; in reality the agent must be installed and running, and the instance must have an IAM instance profile granting ssm actions. Another mistake is assuming that agent installation alone is sufficient — network egress to SSM endpoints and correct system permissions are also required. Key checks are: process running, instance profile attached, and successful registration in the SSM console. Takeaway: verify the agent before building automation, because it is the single point of execution for SSM actions.

keyIdea.text: The agent executes commands and reports back; without it SSM cannot manage the instance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › SSM Agent
Definition

The SSM Agent is the on-instance process that accepts documents and commands from Systems Manager and performs actions locally.

What it sends

Execution output, status, and inventory information back to SSM.

What it receives

Commands, documents, and configuration instructions to apply locally.

Key Takeaway

Verify the agent, instance role, and network egress before relying on automation.

Checks and example
  • Ensure the process is running on the instance and reporting in the SSM console.
  • Confirm the IAM instance profile includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore or equivalent permissions such as ssm:SendMessage.
  • Check that the instance can reach SSM endpoints (network egress) for registration and commands.
Misconception: Installing the agent is enough. In reality you must also attach the instance profile and allow necessary network access.

screens.title: Configuring IAM Instance Profiles for SSM
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM instance profile grants an EC2 instance permissions to call SSM APIs and access Parameter Store. The simplest, recommended managed policy is AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore because it includes the actions the agent needs. To create a reliable setup: first create an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy and any additional least-privilege permissions you require, name it clearly such as SSMManagedInstanceRole, and use that role when launching your EC2 instance. After launch, verify the role is attached in the EC2 console. A common error is launching an instance without attaching an instance profile or attaching an overly-permissive role. For Parameter Store access, add explicit permissions for ssm:GetParameter or ssm:GetParameters if you want the instance to retrieve secure strings. Example: if your application needs a database connection stored in Parameter Store, grant the role permission to read only that parameter path. Another practical check is to attempt a simple SSM A P I call from within the instance or verify it appears as a managed instance in the SSM console. Remember: the agent cannot act without the role; operations will fail silently if permissions are missing, so verify and test in a small environment before scaling.

keyIdea.title: Least-privilege instance profiles
keyIdea.text: Attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and scope additional permissions for Parameter Store to only the parameters needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Instance Profile
Step-by-step
  1. Create IAM role for EC2 and attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  2. Name the role e.g. SSMManagedInstanceRole for clarity.
  3. Launch EC2 and select the instance profile during configuration.
  4. Optionally add fine-grained ssm:GetParameter permissions scoped to parameter ARNs.
Misconception: broad EC2 permissions help debugging. In fact, narrow permissions reduce blast radius and align with least-privilege.
Verification checks
SSM Console: instance appears as managed
Inside instance: agent logs show successful registration
Try a test Run Command to confirm permissions and connectivity
Key Takeaway

Attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and scope additional permissions to required Parameter Store paths only.

screens.title: Run Command: secure remote execution
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command is the capability you use when you need to execute commands or scripts on one or many managed instances without opening SSH or RDP. It uses IAM for authorization and the SSM Agent to run the script locally, and it can capture output to S3 or CloudWatch for auditing. A typical use is installing a package across dozens of instances, restarting a service, or collecting diagnostics. For Linux, use the AWS-RunShellScript document; for Windows use AWS-RunPowerShellScript. For example, to install htop you might specify a command like sudo yum install -y htop for Amazon Linux. One misconception is that Run Command replaces configuration management — it is ideal for ad-hoc or scheduled commands, but for persistent desired state you should use State Manager. Another operational note: always limit target selection using tags or resource groups and send output to a centralized bucket or log group so you can review success and failures. Takeaway: Run Command improves security and scale for remote operations, but pair it with State Manager when you need continuous enforcement. Run Command: secure remote execution means run command runs scripts securely without ssh and captures output for auditing. use tags to scope targets and log outputs centrally.. In practical terms, use run command to run scripts at scale without ssh. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Run Command
How it works
  • Choose a document (AWS-RunShellScript or AWS-RunPowerShellScript).
  • Provide command text and target instances by IDs, tags, or resource groups.
  • Optionally send output to S3 or CloudWatch Logs for auditing.
Misconception: Run Command equals configuration management. Use State Manager for desired state enforcement instead.
Example command
# Using AWS-RunShellScript to install htop on Amazon Linux
sudo yum install -y htop

# For Ubuntu:
sudo apt-get update -y
sudo apt-get install -y htop
Tip

Send command output to CloudWatch or S3 to retain evidence and debug failures.

screens.title: State Manager and Associations
screens.narratorSegment: SSM State Manager enforces a desired configuration by creating associations that apply documents on a schedule or when triggered. An association ties a document — predefined or custom — to a set of targets and optionally a schedule like cron or rate expressions. State Manager will periodically check instances and apply the document when drift is detected, making it ideal for ensuring packages are installed, services are running, or configuration files are present. For example, create an association named NginxInstallationAssociation that references a custom InstallNginxLinux document and targets a set of EC2 instances. You can schedule it to run daily or more frequently for testing. A frequent mistake is deploying associations without testing: if two associations conflict, they can fight over a file or restart services repeatedly. Always test on an isolated group, observe logs, and then roll out. Another practical note is to capture association outputs or send them to CloudWatch for compliance reporting. Takeaway: use State Manager when you need persistent enforcement rather than a one-off change. State Manager and Associations means state manager applies documents on a schedule and corrects drift, ideal for configuration consistency across fleets.. In practical terms, define desired state and keep instances compliant over time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › State Manager
What an association contains
  • Document to apply (predefined or custom).
  • Targets (instance IDs, tags, resource groups).
  • Schedule expression (cron or rate).
  • Parameters and output options (S3/CloudWatch).
Example: Nginx association
Name: NginxInstallationAssociation
Document: InstallNginxLinux
Schedule: cron(0 0 ? * * *) (daily) or rate(30 minutes) for testing
Common mistake

Deploying untested associations or overlapping associations that conflict. Test in isolation first.

screens.title: Authoring a Custom SSM Document (InstallNginxLinux)
screens.narratorSegment: A custom SSM Command document defines the steps the agent will execute on managed instances. Documents use YAML or JSON and typically wrap aws:runShellScript or other plugin actions. I will walk you through the InstallNginxLinux example: it uses schemaVersion 2.2, describes parameters such as action with a default of install, then defines a main step that runs aws:runShellScript with preconditions for the Linux platform. The script performs updates, installs the nginx package using the platform's package manager, enables and starts the service, and prints success messages. A key practice is to include an uninstall path and validate inputs to avoid irreversible changes. Also add preconditions so the document does not run on the wrong platform. Misconception: put everything into a single document. Instead, keep documents focused and idempotent so repeated runs do not cause side effects. We'll show the YAML content so you can copy and test it in the console. After creating the document, test on a single instance and inspect the command output before scaling via State Manager. Authoring a Custom SSM Document (InstallNginxLinux) means create focused, idempotent documents with preconditions, parameters, and clear success/failure paths; test before scaling.. In practical terms, create a command document to install and start nginx on amazon linux. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › InstallNginxLinux
YAML document (create in SSM Documents console)
schemaVersion: '2.2' description: Install and start Nginx on Amazon Linux. parameters: action: type: String description: (Optional) The action to perform (install, uninstall). default: install mainSteps: - action: aws:runShellScript name: installNginx precondition: StringEquals: - platformType - Linux inputs: runCommand: - | #!/bin/bash if [ "{{action}}" == "install" ]; then sudo yum update -y sudo amazon-linux-extras install nginx1 -y sudo systemctl enable nginx sudo systemctl start nginx echo "Nginx installed and started." elif [ "{{action}}" == "uninstall" ]; then sudo systemctl stop nginx sudo systemctl disable nginx sudo yum remove nginx -y echo "Nginx uninstalled." else echo "Invalid action specified: {{action}}" exit 1 fi
Authoring tips
  • Keep documents idempotent so re-running is safe.
  • Add preconditions to avoid running on incorrect platforms.
  • Include parameters with sensible defaults and validation.
  • Test on a single instance and inspect output logs before scaling.
Misconception: automation scripts are one-off. Treat documents as versioned, testable artifacts with clear rollback/uninstall paths.

screens.title: Create a State Manager Association
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an association in State Manager connects a document to a set of instances and defines when it runs. Walk through these steps: first, choose or create the document — for the hands-on lab we use InstallNginxLinux. Second, give the association a clear name, for example NginxInstallationAssociation. Third, select targets: choose instances manually, by tag, or resource group. Manual selection is great for initial testing. Fourth, specify a schedule. Use cron expressions for precise timing or rate expressions for testing; the example suggests cron(0 0? * * *) for daily execution or rate(30 minutes) for testing. Fifth, set parameters (leave action set to install) and decide whether to send output to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs to capture logs for auditing. Finally, create the association and monitor its status. A common mistake is scheduling a frequent run in production without testing, causing repeated restarts or conflicts. Start with a single instance, verify the run and the web page, then gradually expand the target set. This approach reduces risk while achieving automated enforcement. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › State Manager Association
Configuration checklist
  1. Name the association (e.g. NginxInstallationAssociation).
  2. Select the InstallNginxLinux document.
  3. Choose targets: manual instance select for initial testing.
  4. Set schedule: cron or rate expression.
  5. Configure parameters and output (S3/CloudWatch).
Monitoring and verification
After creation, observe association status in State Manager. Check execution logs and the instance's SSM command output. Then verify the web server by visiting the instance public IP and confirming the Nginx welcome page.
Warning

Avoid deploying new associations fleet-wide without testing, as conflicting associations may cause disruption.

screens.title: SSM Automation Documents
screens.narratorSegment: SSM Automation lets you build multi-step workflows that can interact with EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, and SNS. An Automation document is a JSON or YAML description of steps, parameters, and error handling logic. Use Automation when you need to standardize complex operational procedures — for example, create a golden AMI by stopping an instance, creating a snapshot, creating an AMI, and notifying an SNS topic upon completion. An Automation step might call aws:stopInstances, aws:createImage, and a Lambda function for custom processing. Important design choices include parameterizing resource identifiers, adding clear retry and error handling logic, and emitting status to a log or SNS for external monitoring. screens.title: SSM Parameter Store
screens.narratorSegment: Parameter Store is a hierarchical key-value store for configuration and secrets. Parameters can be plain text or SecureString, where SecureString values are encrypted with AWS KMS. Use Parameter Store to avoid hardcoding credentials or environment values into code. For example, store a production database connection string at a path such as /prod/myapp/db-connection and grant only the application instance role permission to read that specific path. This follows the principle of least privilege and reduces accidental exposure. Applications running on EC2 can retrieve parameters via the SDK or CLI; ensure the instance profile has ssm:GetParameter permissions for the parameter ARN. A common misconception is treating Parameter Store like a full secrets manager; while it is suitable for many secrets and integrates with KMS encryption, evaluate rotation and lifecycle needs against other services if required. Takeaway: Parameter Store centralizes configuration, supports encryption, and simplifies secure retrieval at runtime when paired with narrowly scoped IAM roles. screens.title: Run Command vs State Manager vs Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right SSM capability depends on intent. Use Run Command when you need to perform ad-hoc or scheduled commands on one or many instances quickly — for example, to collect diagnostics or apply a one-off patch. Use State Manager when you want persistent enforcement of a desired state: define an association and let SSM correct drift, ensuring a package remains installed or a service stays running. Use Automation when a task spans multiple AWS services or requires multiple ordered steps with parameters and error handling — for example creating AMIs, snapshots, or a controlled remediation workflow. A common misconception is to use Run Command for all automation needs; that leads to fragile, ad-hoc processes that do not self-heal. Conversely, overusing Automation for single-step tasks adds unnecessary complexity. Think: Run Command for one-off execution, State Manager for ongoing compliance, Automation for orchestration across services. Example mapping: patching schedules are best handled by Patch Manager (a specialized SSM feature) or State Manager for recurring enforcement; creating a golden AMI is best with Automation to sequence stop-snapshot-start and notifications. Takeaway: match capability to intent to ensure scalable, maintainable operations.

screens.title: Hands-on: Launch, document, associate, verify
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab ties the pieces together. Part one: create an IAM role named SSMManagedInstanceRole and attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Launch an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance with that instance profile and ensure it has outbound HTTP/HTTPS for package install. Verify the SSM Agent is running and the instance appears as managed in SSM. Part two: create the custom command document InstallNginxLinux in the SSM Documents console with the YAML we saw earlier. Part three: create a State Manager association named NginxInstallationAssociation, target your instance, and schedule it using a cron or rate expression. Leave action parameter as install. Optionally configure output to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs. Part four: after the association runs, obtain the instance public IP and browse to http://. You should see the Nginx welcome page. If you do not, check the security group for port 80, inspect the association execution logs, and validate the agent and role. Misconception: skipping log checks. Always inspect output and logs to confirm success and troubleshoot when things fail. Final takeaway: this sequence converts an ad-hoc install into a repeatable, auditable process.

screens.title: Operational Best Practices & Mistakes to Avoid
screens.narratorSegment: Before you automate at scale, internalize a short checklist. First, always test documents and associations on a small, isolated group of instances; do not roll out untested changes fleet-wide. In this lesson you will master the core pieces of AWS Systems Manager that let you manage large fleets and automate operational work. We'll look at the SSM Agent, how instances authenticate with an IAM instance profile, and four key capabilities: Run Command for remote execution, State Manager for enforcing desired state, Automation for orchestrating multi-step operations, and Parameter Store for secure configuration and secrets. You will see a hands-on pattern: create an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy, launch an EC2 instance with that role and verify the agent, author a small command document to install Nginx, and use State Manager to ensure the web server remains installed and running. This approach reduces manual SSH sessions, lowers your attack surface, and enforces consistency across environments. I will also warn you about common mistakes — forgetting the agent, missing IAM permissions, and untested associations — and show mitigation steps. By the end, you will understand each SSM capability, how they fit together in real operations, and how to apply them safely. What operational pain point will you solve first with SSM?

These objectives guide the practical skills we'll build. First, you will explain the SSM architecture and its core components including the agent and how it communicates with the service. I will demonstrate why the agent and the correct IAM instance profile are required, and give you a small checklist for verification to prevent common pitfalls. Second, you will implement State Manager associations to define and maintain desired state across instances. You'll learn how to author an association, schedule it, and verify compliance so that configuration drift is eliminated. Third, you will use Run Command to run ad-hoc commands and scripts securely on multiple targets; we'll show an example of installing a package and collecting output to S3 or CloudWatch for auditing. Fourth, you will design Automation documents that chain steps across services and include error handling, and you'll integrate Parameter Store to securely store configuration and secrets. Each objective pairs explanation with a hands-on step to practice; by the end you'll not only know the components but be able to use them safely and repeatably.

These additional objectives focus on applying SSM safely. You will verify SSM Agent connectivity and instance profile permissions, learning a short troubleshooting checklist: confirm the agent service is running, check the instance has the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role or equivalent permissions, and validate network egress for the agent. You will also learn to author and test SSM documents in a small group of instances before wide roll-out, preventing conflicting associations or accidental service restarts. Another objective is to capture command output for auditing: send Run Command output to S3 or CloudWatch Logs and inspect it for success or failure messages. Finally, you will practice scheduling associations and Automation runs with cron or rate expressions, and design error handling inside Automation documents. Each objective closes the gap between 'it works once' and 'it works reliably at scale.' You will leave with checklists for safety and compliance to reduce operational risk.

The SSM Agent is a small daemon installed on EC2 instances and supported on some on-premises servers. Its role is simple but critical: it receives messages and documents from the Systems Manager control plane and executes actions on the host. Without the agent, SSM cannot discover or run commands on that instance. In practice you should think of the agent as the managed process that bridges your instance to the SSM service, relaying command inputs, execution progress, and output. For example, when you issue a Run Command to install a package, the SSM Agent runs the shell or PowerShell script and returns the result to the service, which can then forward logs to CloudWatch or S3. A common misconception is that SSM will manage any instance automatically; in reality the agent must be installed and running, and the instance must have an IAM instance profile granting ssm actions. Another mistake is assuming that agent installation alone is sufficient — network egress to SSM endpoints and correct system permissions are also required. Key checks are: process running, instance profile attached, and successful registration in the SSM console. Takeaway: verify the agent before building automation, because it is the single point of execution for SSM actions.

An IAM instance profile grants an EC2 instance permissions to call SSM APIs and access Parameter Store. The simplest, recommended managed policy is AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore because it includes the actions the agent needs. To create a reliable setup: first create an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy and any additional least-privilege permissions you require, name it clearly such as SSMManagedInstanceRole, and use that role when launching your EC2 instance. After launch, verify the role is attached in the EC2 console. A common error is launching an instance without attaching an instance profile or attaching an overly-permissive role. For Parameter Store access, add explicit permissions for ssm:GetParameter or ssm:GetParameters if you want the instance to retrieve secure strings. Example: if your application needs a database connection stored in Parameter Store, grant the role permission to read only that parameter path. Another practical check is to attempt a simple SSM A P I call from within the instance or verify it appears as a managed instance in the SSM console. Remember: the agent cannot act without the role; operations will fail silently if permissions are missing, so verify and test in a small environment before scaling.

Run Command is the capability you use when you need to execute commands or scripts on one or many managed instances without opening SSH or RDP. It uses IAM for authorization and the SSM Agent to run the script locally, and it can capture output to S3 or CloudWatch for auditing. A typical use is installing a package across dozens of instances, restarting a service, or collecting diagnostics. For Linux, use the AWS-RunShellScript document; for Windows use AWS-RunPowerShellScript. For example, to install htop you might specify a command like sudo yum install -y htop for Amazon Linux. One misconception is that Run Command replaces configuration management — it is ideal for ad-hoc or scheduled commands, but for persistent desired state you should use State Manager. Another operational note: always limit target selection using tags or resource groups and send output to a centralized bucket or log group so you can review success and failures. Choosing the right SSM capability depends on intent. Use Run Command when you need to perform ad-hoc or scheduled commands on one or many instances quickly — for example, to collect diagnostics or apply a one-off patch. Use State Manager when you want persistent enforcement of a desired state: define an association and let SSM correct drift, ensuring a package remains installed or a service stays running. Use Automation when a task spans multiple AWS services or requires multiple ordered steps with parameters and error handling — for example creating AMIs, snapshots, or a controlled remediation workflow. A common misconception is to use Run Command for all automation needs; that leads to fragile, ad-hoc processes that do not self-heal. Conversely, overusing Automation for single-step tasks adds unnecessary complexity. Think: Run Command for one-off execution, State Manager for ongoing compliance, Automation for orchestration across services. Example mapping: patching schedules are best handled by Patch Manager (a specialized SSM feature) or State Manager for recurring enforcement; creating a golden AMI is best with Automation to sequence stop-snapshot-start and notifications. Takeaway: match capability to intent to ensure scalable, maintainable operations.

First, the SSM Agent is required on managed instances and must run with an instance profile that grants SSM permissions; without both, management fails. Second, use Run Command for ad-hoc or scheduled executions, State Manager for persistent desired state enforcement through associations, and Automation for multi-step orchestration across services. Choose the capability that matches your intent. Third, Parameter Store centralizes configuration and secrets; use SecureString with KMS and grant least-privilege access to instance roles. Before you automate at scale, internalize a short checklist. First, always test documents and associations on a small, isolated group of instances; do not roll out untested changes fleet-wide. Second, capture execution output centrally using CloudWatch Logs or S3 for auditing and debugging. Third, apply least-privilege IAM: give instance roles only the permissions they need to read specific Parameter Store paths or to perform the actions in a document. Fourth, design Automation documents to be idempotent and include retry and error handling.
